name: Xylitol mints

lead: Xylitol mints are breath mints made with xylitol rather than sugar. Users choose them for fresh breath and saliva stimulation without sugar.
The only direct study is a 2017 laboratory simulator, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found xylitol candy did not reduce plaque the way gum did.

paras: Xylitol is thought to suppress oral streptococci, and sucking a mint stimulates saliva.
High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs.

lead: Xylitol mints are breath mints sweetened with xylitol instead of sugar, used by people who want fresh breath without feeding oral bacteria and who want to stimulate saliva.[1]

Direct evidence is thin. A 2017 laboratory study used a dental simulator to compare commercial xylitol and sucrose mint products on Streptococcus mutans adherence and growth.[1] Wikipedia's xylitol article does not discuss mints specifically, and a 2022 review it cites found that xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque while xylitol candy does not.[2]
infobox: Breath, saliva stimulation, lower sugar exposure

paras: High xylitol intake can cause gas, diarrhea and IBS-like symptoms, and xylitol is toxic to dogs.[2]

No studies found of xylitol mints in people. Related laboratory work: the 2017 dental-simulator study tested 3% solutions of sucrose, xylitol, sucrose mints, xylitol mints and peppermint oil on planktonic and adhered S. mutans.[1] Studies of xylitol chewing gum are covered in a separate article.
